summary: Open-source AI models make frontier tokens MORE valuable, not less — frontier intelligence can orchestrate open-source models, increasing its own value
summary_extended: Baker argues that the proliferation of open-source AI models does not commoditize frontier AI but instead amplifies its value, because frontier models (which he characterizes as '250 IQ') can orchestrate and delegate tasks to cheaper open-source models ('150 IQ'), making the frontier layer more economically indispensable. His core prediction is that frontier tokens will capture 65–85% of total AI economic value even though open-source tokens will represent roughly 80% of total volume — a structural split analogous to how a small number of elite professionals capture disproportionate economic rents. He uses the Manhattan Project as an analogy: Oppenheimer's productivity was multiplied, not diminished, by having a large pool of capable physicists to direct. The investment implication is that companies producing and monetizing frontier models — those at the absolute capability frontier — are structurally undervalued relative to fears about open-source commoditization. This thesis favors pure-play frontier model providers over open-source or commodity inference players.
detail: Baker argues frontier models (250 IQ) that can orchestrate open-source models (150 IQ) are more valuable because they can farm out tasks. He predicts frontier tokens will be 65-85% of economic value while open-source tokens are 80% of volume. Uses Manhattan Project analogy: Oppenheimer needed the broader physicist pool to be productive.
